clue.text: In the end inflammation occurs here

definitions.text: In the end inflammation occurs here

parts.words: In the end inflammation occurs here
parts.note: a little wooden stick whose tip bursts into flame when struck: the 'inflammation' is a literal catching fire, at one end

explanation.surface: A medical note on where an inflamed condition finally breaks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inflammation' reads as a swelling, but here it means bursting into flame, which happens at the head end of this small stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A light for a fire is struck from its tipped end, which is where it ignites.

clue.text: Acts proverbially like wine

parts.note: Proverbs 20:1 says 'Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging', so wine, in the proverb, ridicules

explanation.surface: Wine behaving just as the old sayings say it does.
explanation.walkthrough: The reference is to the Book of Proverbs, 'Wine is a mocker', so to act like wine there is to ridicule.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical proverb calls wine a scoffer, so doing what it does is to ridicule or jeer.

clue.text: So the Calf of Man is a protected area?

definitions.text: So the Calf of Man is a protected area?

parts.words: So the Calf of Man is a protected area?
parts.note: the Calf of Man is a small island off the Isle of Man, but read as the calf of a man's leg it is protected when he wears tall riding boots

explanation.surface: A question about whether a small island off the Isle of Man is a nature reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: The Calf of Man is an islet south of the Isle of Man, so 'protected area' suggests conservation; read instead as a man's lower leg, shielded by tall boots reaching up the shin.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearing high leather riding boots covers the lower leg, so a wearer's leg below the knee is shielded.

clue.text: Post in which the mind rules the body in part

parts.note: the head is where the mind sits, so it stands for it
to master is to control or rule
the hip is one part of the body

explanation.surface: A job description in which intellect dominates the physical self.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like philosophy of mind over body; it is a charade of three words, the last a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: The role of running a school is an appointment, and a post is a job or appointment.

clue.text: So many tutors have physical bonds !

parts.note: a vague quantity standing for a number, here ten
dons are university teachers or tutors

explanation.surface: Lots of college tutors share a physical closeness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So many' is a stock crossword way of indicating a number, here TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Fibrous cords join muscle to bone, so they are the body's literal ties.

clue.text: Early riser in Channel Islands gets a flower

indicators.note: the bird is placed inside the abbreviation for the islands

parts.note: CI is the abbreviation for the Channel Islands, off the coast of Normandy
the lark is proverbially up at dawn, so an early riser

explanation.surface: Someone who gets up early on Jersey or Guernsey is given a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early riser' sounds like a person but is the lark, a bird that sings at dawn.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a genus of annual garden plants with showy blooms, named after the explorer William Clark.

clue.text: A haircut for the Corporal

explanation.surface: A soldier being given a short back and sides.
explanation.walkthrough: Corporal Trim is a character in Laurence Sterne's eighteenth-century novel Tristram Shandy.
explanation.definitionFit: A light tidy-up of the hair is one sense; Corporal Trim is Uncle Toby's servant in Sterne's novel Tristram Shandy.

clue.text: It goes round or uphill

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill; in a down clue, written going up, its letters run bottom to top
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something that either circles or climbs a slope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uphill' is a single word doing the work of a hill (TOR, a Dartmoor-style rocky peak) written upwards in this down entry; the clue names 'or' first but it comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotating part of a machine, such as a helicopter blade assembly, spins about an axis.

clue.text: Suspects fog causes oxidation

parts.note: mist is a thin fog
rust forms by oxidation of iron, so something that rusts oxidises

explanation.surface: Someone suspects that damp fog makes metal corrode.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a sentence with 'Suspects' as a verb about fog; the answer splits into the weather word and the corrosion word.
explanation.definitionFit: To doubt someone's honesty is to distrust them, which is what suspecting is.

clue.text: Literary man who mounted a haystack without purpose

parts.note: rode means sat on and rode a horse, i.e. mounted
a rick is a stack of hay
random means aimless, done without purpose

explanation.surface: A writer aimlessly climbed onto a pile of hay.
explanation.walkthrough: The title character of Tobias Smollett's 1748 picaresque novel, built from three plain words.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the hero of Smollett's eighteenth-century novel, so a figure from fiction.

clue.text: Henley's rank of soul

parts.note: W. E. Henley's poem Invictus ends 'I am the master of my fate, I am the ... of my soul', naming a commanding rank

explanation.surface: A question about the title a poet gives to his inner self.
explanation.walkthrough: Henley's poem Invictus closes with 'I am the master of my fate, / I am the [rank] of my soul'; the rank is the one who commands a ship or team.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's last line names a commander's rank, the one in charge of a ship, as the speaker's role toward his soul.

clue.text: An extremely painful condition is found in little animals

parts.note: an gives the letter A
gout is a notoriously painful inflammation of the joints

explanation.surface: Tiny creatures are discovered to suffer from a very painful ailment.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'little'; the text was read as 'kittle'. Gout in old cartoons is the rich man's painful toe.
explanation.definitionFit: These are small South American burrowing rodents, related to guinea pigs.

clue.text: Thrush that will attack a rooster

parts.note: to storm is to attack violently
a cock is a male fowl, a rooster

explanation.surface: A songbird that will go for a farmyard cockerel.
explanation.walkthrough: A country name for the mistle thrush, which sings in stormy weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Old country name for the mistle thrush, a large songbird of the thrush family.

clue.text: A source of Shakespearian comedy

parts.note: one of Shakespeare's plays is The Comedy of ..., so a mistake, one of many, is the source of that comedy

explanation.surface: A remark about where Shakespeare got his funny material.
explanation.walkthrough: The Comedy of Errors is the Shakespeare play of mistaken twins, so a single blunder is one source of that comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A mistake or blunder; Shakespeare's play is The Comedy of Errors, built on many of them.

clue.text: Sometimes crazy ways of pedestrians

parts.note: walkers' routes, and 'crazy paving' gives garden walks laid in irregular slabs, so these are sometimes crazy

explanation.surface: A grumble about the mad behaviour of people on foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy' seems to describe the pedestrians' behaviour, but refers to crazy paving, walks laid with irregular broken slabs.
explanation.definitionFit: Tracks or footways made for walkers are the routes they take, sometimes laid as crazy paving.

clue.text: Trap egg in novel plasterwork

indicators.note: novel means new, so these letters are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A trap for eggs inside a work of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book that holds the trap, but is the signal to rearrange TRAP, EGG and IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorative ornamental plaster on a building's exterior walls, common on old timber-framed houses.

clue.text: Scratches and leaves marks if that is included

indicators.note: the conditional word and the Latin abbreviation are put inside the word for wound marks

parts.note: to scar is to leave marks on skin
taken as written
ie is the Latin abbreviation id est, that is

explanation.surface: An injury scratches and leaves marks, if that is part of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' looks like foliage or departing, but goes with 'marks' as a verb phrase: to scar.
explanation.definitionFit: To score or lightly cut the surface of skin or soil is to scratch it.

clue.text: It may be in Pope, but it's not at all fair

parts.note: taken as written
Clement is the name of several popes

explanation.surface: Something found in the poet Alexander Pope is decidedly unjust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pope' suggests the poet, but it is a pontiff named Clement, with IN before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Weather that is harsh, stormy and cold is the opposite of fine.

clue.text: Final demand day ?

parts.note: an overdue bill's last reminder was traditionally printed in crimson ink, and saints' feast days were marked in crimson in church calendars, giving a phrase for a memorable occasion

explanation.surface: Wondering when the last bill reminder will arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: Final demands were printed in red, and church calendars printed saints' days in red, giving the phrase for a special day.
explanation.definitionFit: Feast days were printed in crimson in old calendars, hence a notable day; final bill demands are also printed in crimson.

clue.text: There's point in a Norman saint

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe
E for east is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A Norman holy woman has a point to make.
explanation.walkthrough: St Thérèse of Lisieux lived in Normandy; 'point' is a compass point, E.
explanation.definitionFit: Ste Thérèse, the 'Little Flower', was a Carmelite nun at Lisieux in Normandy.

clue.text: Have second misgivings about field-work

explanation.surface: Someone has second thoughts about a military earthwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'field-work' is a military term for a temporary fortification built in the field, not agricultural or research work.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as re-doubt it means to question again; separately it is a small enclosed earthwork fortification.

clue.text: Thrills which, au fond, are painful

explanation.surface: Excitements that, at bottom, actually hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'au fond' is French for 'basically', but read literally as 'at the bottom': blows from a boot to the backside are painful.
explanation.definitionFit: Excitements are one sense; blows from a boot, au fond meaning at the bottom, hurt the behind.

clue.text: Those of essential spirit

indicators.note: the answer is made of, formed from, the letters of the word before it

explanation.surface: Those who belong to a fundamental spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearrangement is signalled only by 'of', read as 'made out of' THOSE; old Times clues were looser with indicators.
explanation.definitionFit: The characteristic spirit or guiding beliefs of a community or era.

clue.text: Make Winnie turn up, Bob, for bowling

indicators.note: in a down clue the bear's name is turned upward, so read from bottom to top

parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh, A. A. Milne's bear
a bob was a shilling in old British money, abbreviated s

explanation.surface: A request to get Winnie and Bob to show up for a game of bowls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn up' reverses POOH, then S follows. Children once bowled hoops along with a stick; a bob was a pre-decimal British shilling, written s.
explanation.definitionFit: Large rings were once bowled along the street by children with a stick, so they are things for bowling.

clue.text: Voluminous sheets for undercover purposes

parts.note: leaves found in volumes, i.e. books, just inside the cover, pasted to the boards

explanation.surface: Large bedsheets intended for secret agents or for getting under the covers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Voluminous' sounds like 'very large', but means belonging to a volume; 'undercover' is literally under the book's cover.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the blank leaves at the front and back of a book, glued just inside its binding.

clue.text: Apart from sewing a sister's use is questionable

indicators.note: something questionable is doubtful or open to change, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Apart from her needlework, a nun's usefulness is in doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: The music-hall song 'Sister Susie's Sewing Shirts for Soldiers' gives the name; 'questionable' rearranges USE IS.
explanation.definitionFit: In the 1914 song, the needlewoman sibling is named in 'Sister Susie's sewing shirts for soldiers'.

clue.text: I do have lies circulated, love, too much

indicators.note: lies spread around are scattered, so these letters are moved about

explanation.surface: Someone whose falsehoods get around is loved excessively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circulated' looks like rumours spreading but rearranges I DO and LIES.
explanation.definitionFit: To worship someone excessively is to adore them more than is wise.

clue.text: Strip, off uniform

explanation.surface: Someone removes their uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: In the forces, 'undress' means everyday uniform rather than full dress.
explanation.definitionFit: To take one's clothes off is one sense; in the military it is ordinary, non-ceremonial uniform as opposed to full dress.

clue.text: Point to canonized doughboy

parts.note: doughboy was slang for an American infantryman, a GI
ST is the abbreviation for saint, one who has been canonized

explanation.surface: Pointing towards a soldier who has been made a saint.
explanation.walkthrough: A doughboy is an American soldier of the First World War, later called a GI.
explanation.definitionFit: The main point of an argument is its essence or substance.

clue.text: Time in the middle for a short space

indicators.note: the time word is placed inside the word for middle

parts.note: centre means middle
taken as written

explanation.surface: A brief pause in the middle for a short interval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time' goes inside CENTRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A hundredth of a metre is a small distance, so a short space.
